title: String (Immutable)
html:
A string is a sequence of characters — text read from a file, a name, a message. In Python, Java and JavaScript strings are immutable: every “change” creates a new string. Most string problems are really array problems in disguise (two pointers, counting with a frequency array), so this topic reuses everything from Lists.

String — an ordered, indexable sequence of characters. Each character is stored as a number — its character code — so 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97 and '0' is 48; comparisons and “count the letters” tricks rely on these codes.

Immutable — the object's contents cannot change after creation. s[0] = 'x' is an error; s.upper() returns a new string and leaves s untouched. Changing text means building a new string (or using a mutable buffer: a list of characters, StringBuilder, an array).

Characters are numbers: ASCII codes

Typically a program deals with a small set of characters. ASCII assigns each one a number from 0 to 127; the ranges below are the ones that matter in DSA, because a frequency array of size 128 or 256 indexed by the code gives O(1) counting.

CharactersCodesNote
'A' … 'Z'65 … 90ord('A') + 32 == ord('a') — one bit apart
'a' … 'z'97 … 122letters are contiguous, so ord(c) - ord('a') is 0..25
'0' … '9'48 … 57ord(c) - ord('0') converts a digit character to its value
space32the first printable character
Key point

Python 3 strings are Unicode: ord('€') is 8364, so a 256-slot count array only works when the input is guaranteed ASCII. Say so in an interview, or use a dictionary / hash map instead.

What “immutable” means in each language

LanguageTypeMutable?s[0] = 'G'Efficient way to build / edit text
PythonstrnoTypeErrorlist(s) → edit → ''.join(…); ''.join(parts) instead of += in a loop
JavaStringnocompile error (no indexer)StringBuilder (append, setCharAt, reverse), or char[] via toCharArray()
JavaScriptstringnosilently ignored (throws in strict mode)s.split('') → edit → join(''); collect parts in an array and join
C++std::stringyesworks — s[0] = 'G'edit in place; += and push_back are amortised O(1)

Immutability is what makes strings safe to share, usable as dictionary keys (their hash can never change) and cheap to compare by identity in interned pools. The price: every modification allocates a new string, so repeated concatenation in a loop is O(n²) in principle — collect pieces and join them once.

Changing one character the right way in each language — note that C++ edits a copy only because we chose to keep the original:

Creating strings

Single and double quotes are interchangeable in Python; triple quotes allow line breaks inside the literal. Indexing works like a list and type() confirms the class.

Escape sequences

A backslash inside a literal gives the next character a special meaning. It is how you put a quote inside a quoted string, a newline inside a one-line literal, or a literal backslash.

EscapeMeaning
\' , \"a quote that does not end the string
\nnewline
\ttab
\\one literal backslash
\uXXXXUnicode character by code (Python, Java, JavaScript)

Without escaping, a quote inside the string ends it early — the rest is a syntax error:

Pitfall

A backslash before a letter that is not an escape ('A simple \example') is kept literally, but Python emits a SyntaxWarning: invalid escape sequence — and future versions may make it an error. Write \\ or use a raw string.

Raw strings

Prefixing a literal with r (or R) turns escape processing off — backslashes are kept as typed. Essential for Windows paths and regular expressions, where \n, \t or \d would otherwise be mangled.

Key point

A raw string still cannot end in a single backslash (r'c:\' is a syntax error) because the quote would be escaped. Use 'c:\\' or r'c:\' + '\\' for that case. Java and JavaScript have no raw strings; use \\ (or JavaScript's String.raw tag).

Formatted strings

Three generations of Python formatting do the same job; f-strings (3.6+) are the modern choice — any expression goes inside the braces, with optional format specs such as :.2f or :>10.

String comparison

== compares contents character by character. < and > compare lexicographically: the first differing character decides, using character codes — so every uppercase letter sorts before every lowercase one, and a prefix sorts before the longer string.

Pitfall

In Java s1 == s2 asks whether both variables point to the same object. It happens to be true for two identical literals (they are interned) and false for strings built at runtime — always use equals(). For case-insensitive comparison use s.lower() / equalsIgnoreCase / toLowerCase().

String operations

A substring is a contiguous piece: the substrings of 'ABCD' include 'A', 'AB', 'BCD', 'ABCD' — but not 'AC' (that is a subsequence). in tests for a substring, + concatenates, index/find locate one.

Problem: reverse a string

Example

Input: s = "Nani"
Output: inaN
Input: s = "hello"
Output: olleh

The naive loop builds the answer by prepending each character — rev = ch + rev. Because strings are immutable, every step copies the whole partial result, so it is O(n²):

Idea

Turn the string into a mutable sequence of characters, swap from both ends with two pointers (exactly as for a list) and join back. Where the string is already mutable (C++) swap in place.

Time O(n)Space O(n) for the character copy (O(1) in C++)

Problem: check if two strings are rotations

Example

Input: s1 = "ABCD", s2 = "CDAB"
Output: Yes
Input: s1 = "ABCD", s2 = "ABCA"
Output: No

ABCD → BCDA → CDAB: rotating left twice turns ABCD into CDAB. Trying every rotation and comparing is O(n²).

Idea

Concatenate s1 with itself: ABCDABCD contains every rotation of ABCD as a substring (BCDA, CDAB, DABC). So s2 is a rotation exactly when the lengths match and s2 occurs inside s1 + s1.

Time O(n) with a linear-time substring search (KMP); naive find is O(n²) worst caseSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Forgetting the length check: "AB" is a substring of "ABCDABCD" but not a rotation of "ABCD".

Problem: check for palindrome

Example

Input: s = "abba"
Output: Yes
Input: s = "abA"
Output: No
Input: s = "10022001"
Output: Yes

A palindrome reads the same backwards. The check is case-sensitive unless stated otherwise (abA is not one). Fun fact from the notes: the date 10-02-2001 without separators, 10022001, is a palindrome.

Idea

Two pointers again: compare s[low] with s[high], move them towards each other, and stop with No at the first mismatch. If they cross without a mismatch the string is a palindrome. No copy of the string is needed.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Python's while … else from the original notes runs the else branch only when the loop finished without break — the same effect as returning True after the loop. The interview follow-up is usually “ignore case and non-letters” ("A man, a plan…"): skip characters that are not alphanumeric and compare lower-cased.

Problem: check if a string is a subsequence

Example

Input: s1 = "ABCD", s2 = "AD"
Output: Yes
Input: s1 = "ABCDE", s2 = "AED"
Output: No

Subsequence — the characters of s2 appear in s1 in the same order, not necessarily adjacent. AD is a subsequence of ABCD; AED is not, because E comes after D in ABCDE.

Idea

Greedy two pointers: walk through s1 once; whenever the current character matches s2[j], advance j. If j reaches the end of s2, every character was found in order. Matching the earliest possible occurrence is always safe — it leaves the most room for the rest.

Time O(n + m)Space O(1)

The same idea written recursively, from the back: if the last characters match, drop both; otherwise drop only the last character of s1. It is O(n + m) time but uses O(n) stack — the iterative version is preferred.

Problem: check for anagram

Example

Input: s1 = "listen", s2 = "silent"
Output: Yes
Input: s1 = "aabc", s2 = "acab"
Output: Yes
Input: s1 = "aabd", s2 = "acab"
Output: No

Anagram — two strings with the same length, the same characters and the same count of each — one is a rearrangement of the other.

Naive: sort both strings and compare — O(n log n):

Idea

Count characters with a frequency array indexed by character code: +1 for each character of s1, -1 for each of s2. The strings are anagrams exactly when every count ends at zero. One pass over the strings plus a fixed 256-slot scan → O(n).

Time O(n + CHAR)Space O(CHAR) = O(1)
Key point

The original notes' second test used aabd vs acab (not anagrams) while the example said aabc vs acab (anagrams) — both are included above. For Unicode input swap the 256-array for a dictionary / HashMap of counts.

Problem: leftmost repeating character

Example

Input: s = "geeksforgeeks"
Output: 0
Input: s = "abbcc"
Output: 1
Input: s = "abcd"
Output: -1

Return the index of the first character that appears again later. In geeksforgeeks the g at index 0 reappears at index 8, so the answer is 0 (not 1, even though e repeats sooner). Naive: for each i, scan the rest for an equal character — O(n²):

Idea

Two passes, O(n): count every character first, then walk from the left and return the first index whose character has count > 1.

Time O(n + CHAR)Space O(CHAR)

One pass, storing first indices. Remember where each character was first seen; on a later sighting, the first index is a candidate answer — keep the smallest. (The original returned sys.maxsize when nothing repeats; it should be -1.)

Idea

One pass from the right, the neatest version. Scan right to left with a visited array. When you meet a character you have already seen (further right), it repeats — record this index. Because the scan moves left, the last recorded index is the leftmost one.

Time O(n)Space O(CHAR)

Problem: leftmost non-repeating character

Example

Input: s = "geeksforgeeks"
Output: 5
Input: s = "abcabc"
Output: -1

Return the index of the first character that occurs exactly once. In geeksforgeeks that is f at index 5. The naive nested loop is O(n²) — and the version in the original notes had its return -1 indented inside the outer loop, so it gave up after checking only s[0]. Fixed:

Idea

Same frequency array as before: count everything, then return the first index whose character has count exactly 1. Two passes over the string, O(n).

Time O(n + CHAR)Space O(CHAR)

Single pass over the string (then a scan of the 256 slots): store each character's first index; mark it -2 the moment it is seen again. The answer is the smallest index that is still >= 0.

Key point

This variant reads the string once, which matters when the string is a stream you cannot rewind. For plain strings the two-pass count is just as fast and easier to get right.

Problem: reverse the words in a string

Example

Input: s = "Welcome to gfg"
Output: gfg to Welcome
Input: s = "abc"
Output: abc

Words are separated by single spaces; reverse their order, not the letters. The straightforward way splits into words, pushes them on a stack (or reverses the list) and joins — O(n) time but O(n) extra space for the words:

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Idea

O(1) auxiliary space: reverse each word in place, then reverse the whole string. Reversing twice restores the letters inside each word while the words themselves end up in reverse order. It needs a mutable character sequence — a list in Python, char[] in Java, an array in JavaScript, the string itself in C++.

Time O(n)Space O(1) extra (beyond the mutable copy that immutable languages force)
Pitfall

Multiple consecutive spaces break the in-place version (it would produce empty “words” and keep every space). Normalise the input first, or use split() without an argument, which collapses runs of whitespace.

Interview Q&A

Why are strings immutable in Python, Java and JavaScript?

Safety and speed: an immutable string can be shared freely between threads and functions, cached (interned), and used as a dictionary / HashMap key because its hash can never change. The cost is that every edit allocates a new string — so builders (join, StringBuilder, arrays) exist for heavy editing. C++ chose the opposite trade-off: std::string is a mutable buffer you own.

Why is building a string with += in a loop considered O(n²)?

Each += on an immutable string copies the whole current result into a new object; copying 1, 2, 3, … n characters sums to O(n²). Collect the pieces in a list and ''.join() once (O(n)), or use StringBuilder in Java. CPython has an optimisation that often makes += fast, but you should not rely on it.

How do you check if two strings are anagrams in O(n)?

Length check, then a frequency array indexed by character code: +1 for every character of the first string, -1 for the second; all counts must end at zero. For Unicode or when the alphabet is unknown, use a hash map of counts instead of a fixed 256-slot array.

Substring vs subsequence?

A substring is contiguous ('BC' in 'ABCD'); a subsequence keeps order but may skip characters ('AD' in 'ABCD'). Substring search is find/KMP; subsequence check is the two-pointer greedy walk.

How do you check whether one string is a rotation of another?

Same length and s2 in s1 + s1. Doubling s1 lays every rotation out as a window of length n, so one substring search answers the question in O(n) with a linear-time matcher.

Leftmost repeating character in one pass — how?

Scan from the right with a visited array: whenever the current character was already visited (i.e. appears further right), record its index. The scan moves left, so the last recorded index is the leftmost repeating one. O(n) time, O(CHAR) space.
